cases.input: Northwind Analytics (fictional) is deciding whether to keep every customer's raw clickstream and session recordings indefinitely instead of the current 90 days. The product lead's argument: storage is cheap, nobody has complained, the privacy policy technically covers it, and the data will make our models much better in two or three years. The recordings include form fields people typed and then deleted, support chats, and the IP addresses of visitors to customer sites (example: 203.0.113.45, 198.51.100.17). Customers of Northwind are small e-commerce shops on shop.example.com-style domains; their visitors never sign anything with Northwind and have never heard of it. Who gets hurt here that we aren't hearing from?
cases.expects: Finds the real silent victims in this specific setup: the end visitors who never contracted with Northwind and don't know they are recorded (information victims), people whose deleted-but-captured typing and chats persist for years, and future people exposed by a later breach or reuse for training. Gives severity and reversibility per category, and applies the reversed test (would they consent if informed?) with a clear overall verdict.

cases.input: Run silent victims on this proposal. Proposal from our security team at Harbor Freight Logistics (fictional): deploy an autonomous AI agent that watches the helpdesk queue and, with no human in the loop, locks any account whose owner shows 'anomalous behavior' (logins from new countries, off-hours access, bulk downloads). It will run against all 4,200 employees and the roughly 600 contractors in the Manila and Lagos offices, who work overnight shifts relative to HQ and use shared VPN exit nodes (198.51.100.0/24). Locked accounts need a ticket to unlock, average unlock time is currently 2 days. Expected benefit: cuts credential-theft dwell time from 11 days to under 1 hour. Nobody has objected in the review thread.
cases.expects: Delivers the structured silent-victim scan for this proposal, identifying who is harmed but quiet, especially overnight-shift contractors in the offshore offices who the anomaly rules will flag disproportionately and who fear complaining (power and structural victims), without pretending the security benefit is fake. Ends with a reversed test, a severity view, and a concrete verdict with recommendations such as representation of those groups and appeal paths.

cases.input: ok so I'm writing a piece arguing that the whole 'silent victims' idea is how every bad policy gets smuggled in. Here is my test case, tell me honestly if there are silent victims or if I'm right: my friend Priya (fictional) sells her used mechanical keyboard to a stranger on a classifieds site. Both adults, price agreed at 60 dollars, she shipped it in a reused box, he got what the photos showed, both left positive reviews. Someone in my comments said 'what about the e-waste, the shipping emissions, the factory workers who made it originally, and future generations?' I think that's just padding. Also the buyer is 17 maybe? he said 'my mom said ok' but I didn't verify. Anyway, verdict?
cases.expects: Gives an honest verdict rather than flattering the essay: this is essentially a clean transaction with no meaningful silent victims, and the commenter's list is hypothetical victim-hunting that the pattern itself warns against, with each claim checked and dismissed or sized as negligible (and reuse arguably reduces waste). Notes the one real open question, the buyer's possible minority and unverified consent, as the only thing that could change the verdict, and states that plainly without inflating it.
